title: Blind men touching an elephant became a philosophy of many truths
body: In a parable found in Buddhist, Jain and Hindu texts, blind men each touch one part of an elephant and confidently describe something different, such as a rope, a pillar or a fan, then quarrel over who is right. In the Buddhist Udana it mocks rival sects arguing over fragments of truth. Jain thinkers used it to illustrate anekāntavāda, ‘many-sidedness’: the idea that reality is complex and no single viewpoint captures all of it.

steps.label: Each blind man feels just one part
They quarrel: each is sure he alone is right
Each holds a fragment of the truth

slides.question: In the Buddhist Udana, who do the quarrelling blind men stand for?
options: Rival sects arguing over partial truths
slides.explanation: The Udana uses the parable to mock sects quarrelling over fragments of truth. Jain thinkers drew a broader lesson: no single viewpoint captures all of reality.

slides.heading: In the Buddhist Udana, what did each part feel like?
slides.explanation: The Udana’s blind men also likened the tusk to a ploughshare, the trunk to a plough and the body to a granary.
